title: Real Cosine Function is Bounded
theorem_text: $\size {\cos x} \le 1$
proof_text:
From the algebraic definition of the real cosine function:
$\displaystyle \cos x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac {x^{2 n} } {\paren {2 n}!}$
it follows that $\cos x$ is a real function.
Thus $\cos^2 x \ge 0$.
From Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine, we have that $\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x = 1$.
Thus it follows that:
$\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x \le 1$
From Ordering of Squares in Reals and the definition of absolute value, we have that:
$x^2 \le 1 \iff \size x \le 1$
The result follows.
review_reason: Since real sine has nonnegative square, the sum-of-squares identity bounds the cosine square by one, hence the absolute cosine by one.

title: Boundedness of Sine X over X
theorem_text:
Let $x \in \R$.
Then:
$\size {\dfrac {\sin x} x} \le 1$
proof_text:
From Derivative of Sine Function, we have:
$D_x \paren {\sin x} = \cos x$
So by the Mean Value Theorem, there exists $\xi \in \R$ between $0$ and $x$ such that:
$\dfrac {\sin x - \sin 0} {x - 0} = \cos \xi$
From Real Cosine Function is Bounded we have that:
$\size {\cos \xi} \le 1$
review_reason: The mean value quotient divides by x and requires two distinct endpoints. The statement includes x=0 without defining a continuous extension there.

title: Differentiable Bounded Convex Real Function is Constant
theorem_text:
Let $f$ be a real function which is:
$(1): \quad$ Differentiable on $\R$
$(2): \quad$ Bounded on $\R$
$(3): \quad$ Convex on $\R$.
Then $f$ is constant.
proof_text:
Let $f$ be differentiable and bounded on $\R$.
Let $f$ be convex on $\R$.
Let $\xi \in \R$.
Aiming for a contradiction, suppose $f' \left({\xi}\right) > 0$.
Then by Mean Value of Convex Real Function it follows that:
$f \left({x}\right) \ge f \left({\xi}\right) + f' \left({\xi}\right) \left({x - \xi}\right) \to + \infty$ as $x \to +\infty$
and therefore is not bounded.
Similarly, suppose $f' \left({\xi}\right) < 0$.
Then by Mean Value of Convex Real Function it follows that:
$f \left({x}\right) \ge f \left({\xi}\right) + f' \left({\xi}\right) \left({x - \xi}\right) \to + \infty$ as $x \to -\infty$
and therefore is likewise not bounded.
Hence $f' \left({\xi}\right) = 0$.
From Zero Derivative implies Constant Function, it follows that $f$ is constant.
review_reason: The supporting tangent at any point with nonzero derivative grows without bound in one direction. Boundedness forces the derivative to vanish everywhere, hence the function is constant.

title: Equidecomposability is Equivalence Relation
theorem_text: The property of being equidecomposable is an equivalence relation on the power set $\mathcal P \left({\R^n}\right)$.
proof_text:
Relexivity
A set is necessarily equidecomposable with itself; the same decomposition and set of isometries suffice for $A$ as for $A$.
Symmetry
There is no order to the relation of being equidecomposable; symmetry follows.
Transitivity
Suppose $A, B, C \subset \R^n$ are sets such that $A, B$ are equidecomposable and $B, C$ are equidecomposable.
Let $X_1, \dots, X_m$ be a decomposition of $A, B$ together with isometries $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_m, \nu_1, \dots, \nu_m:\R^n \to \R^n$ such that:
$\displaystyle A = \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^m \mu_i \left({X_i}\right)$
and
$\displaystyle B = \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^m \nu_i \left({X_i}\right)$
Further let $Y_1, \dots, Y_p$ together with $\xi_1, \dots, \xi_p, \tau_1, \dots, \tau_p$ be sets and isometries such that:
$\displaystyle B = \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^p \xi_i \left({Y_i}\right)$
and:
$\displaystyle C = \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^p \tau_i \left({Y_i}\right)$
Consider the sets
$Z_{i,j} = \nu_i \left({X_i}\right) \cap \xi_j \left({Y_j}\right)$
where $1 \le i \le m$ and $1 \le j \le p$.
We have:
$\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^m \bigcup_{j \mathop = 1}^p \left({\mu_i \circ \nu_i^{-1}}\right) \left({Z_{i,j}}\right) = \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^m \bigcup_{j \mathop = 1}^p \left({\mu_i \circ \nu_i^{-1}}\right) \left({\nu_i \left({X_i}\right) \cap \xi_j \left({Y_j}\right)}\right) = \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^m \left({\mu_i \circ \nu_i^{-1} \circ \nu_i}\right) \left({X_i}\right) = \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^m \mu_i \left({X_i}\right) = A$
$\displaystyle \bigcup_{j \mathop = 1}^p \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^m \left({\tau_j \circ \xi_j^{-1}}\right) \left({Z_{i,j}}\right) = \bigcup_{j \mathop = 1}^p \bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^m \left({\tau_j \circ \xi_j^{-1}}\right) \left({\nu_i \left({X_i}\right) \cap \xi_j \left({Y_j}\right)}\right) = \bigcup_{j \mathop = 1}^p \left({\tau_j \circ \xi_j^{-1} \circ \xi_j}\right) \left({Y_j}\right) = \bigcup_{j \mathop = 1}^p \tau_j \left({Y_j}\right) = C$
so $Z_{i, j}$ together with the isometries $\mu_i \circ \nu_i^{-1}, \tau_j \circ \xi_j^{-1}$ is a decomposition of $A$ and $C$.
Hence these two are equidecomposable.
review_reason: Intersecting the two finite decompositions of B gives a common disjoint refinement that the composed isometries carry onto pieces of A and C. Identity and interchange of the two sides give reflexivity and symmetry.

title: Derivative of Tangent Function
theorem_text:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\tan x} = \sec^2 x = \dfrac 1 {\cos^2 x}$
when $\cos x \ne 0$.
proof_text:
From the definition of the tangent function:
$\tan x = \dfrac {\sin x} {\cos x}$
From Derivative of Sine Function:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\sin x} = \cos x$
From Derivative of Cosine Function:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\cos x} = -\sin x$
Then:
$$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\tan x} = \frac {\cos x \cos x - \sin x \paren {-\sin x} } {\cos^2 x}$$
Quotient Rule for Derivatives
$$= \frac {\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x} {\cos^2 x}$$
$$= \frac 1 {\cos^2 x}$$
Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine
This is valid only when $\cos x \ne 0$.
The result follows from the Secant is Reciprocal of Cosine.
review_reason: The quotient rule on sin(x)/cos(x) yields the sum of the squared sine and cosine over cosine squared, with the required nonzero denominator.

title: Derivative of Cotangent Function
theorem_text:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\cot x} = -\csc^2 x = \dfrac {-1} {\sin^2 x}$
where $\sin x \ne 0$.
proof_text:
From the definition of the cotangent function:
$\cot x = \dfrac {\cos x} {\sin x}$
From Derivative of Sine Function:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\sin x} = \cos x$
From Derivative of Cosine Function:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\cos x}= -\sin x$
Then:
$$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\cot x} = \frac {\sin x \paren {-\sin x} - \cos x \cos x} {\sin^2 x}$$
Quotient Rule for Derivatives
$$= \frac {-\paren {\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x} } {\sin^2 x}$$
$$= \frac {-1} {\sin^2 x}$$
Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine
This is valid only when $\sin x \ne 0$.
The result follows from the definition of the real cosecant function.
review_reason: Differentiating cosine divided by sine gives minus the sum of their squares over sine squared. The domain condition permits the division.

title: Derivative of Secant Function
theorem_text:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\sec x} = \sec x \tan x$
where $\cos x \ne 0$.
proof_text:
From the definition of the secant function:
$\sec x = \dfrac 1 {\cos x} = \paren {\cos x}^{-1}$
From Derivative of Cosine Function:
$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\cos x} = -\sin x$
Then:
$$\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\sec x} = \map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\paren {\cos x}^{-1} }$$
Exponent Laws
$$= \paren {-\sin x} \paren {-\cos^{-2} x}$$
Chain Rule for Derivatives, Power Rule
$$= \frac 1 {\cos x} \frac {\sin x} {\cos x}$$
Exponent Laws
$$= \sec x \tan x$$
Definitions of secant and tangent
This is valid only when $\cos x \ne 0$.
review_reason: The reciprocal power rule and the derivative of cosine give sine divided by cosine squared, which factors as secant times tangent.

title: Derivative of Arcsine Function
theorem_text: $\dfrac {\map \d {\arcsin x} } {\d x} = \dfrac 1 {\sqrt {1 - x^2} }$
proof_text:
Let $y = \arcsin x$ where $-1 < x < 1$.
Then:
$x = \sin y$
Then from Derivative of Sine Function:
$\dfrac {\d x} {\d y} = \cos y$
Hence from Derivative of Inverse Function:
$\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \dfrac 1 {\cos y}$
From Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine, we have:
$\cos^2 y + \sin^2 y = 1 \implies \cos y = \pm \sqrt {1 - \sin^2 y}$
Now $\cos y \ge 0$ on the image of $\arcsin x$, that is:
$y \in \closedint {-\dfrac \pi 2} {\dfrac \pi 2}$
Thus it follows that we need to take the positive root of $\sqrt {1 - \sin^2 y}$.
So:
$$\frac {\d y} {\d x} = \frac 1 {\sqrt {1 - \sin^2 y} }$$
$$= \frac 1 {\sqrt {1 - x^2} }$$
review_reason: On the interior of the real arcsine domain, the derivative of sine is nonzero on the principal branch, where its cosine is the positive square root.

title: Derivative of Arccosine Function
theorem_text: $\map {D_x} {\arccos x} = \dfrac {-1} {\sqrt {1 - x^2}}$
proof_text:
Let $y = \arccos x$ where $-1 < x < 1$.
Then:
$x = \cos y$
Then from Derivative of Cosine Function:
$\dfrac {\d x} {\d y} = -\sin y$
Hence from Derivative of Inverse Function:
$\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \dfrac {-1} {\sin y}$
From Sum of Squares of Sine and Cosine, we have:
$\cos^2 y + \sin^2 y = 1 \implies \sin y = \pm \sqrt {1 - \cos^2 y}$
Now $\sin y \ge 0$ on the range of $\arccos x$, that is, for $y \in \closedint 0 \pi$.
Thus it follows that we need to take the positive root of $\sqrt {1 - \cos^2 y}$.
So:
$\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \dfrac {-1} {\sqrt {1 - \cos^2 y} }$
and hence the result.
review_reason: For interior x the principal angle lies strictly between zero and pi. Its positive sine determines the sign in the inverse-function derivative.

title: Sum of Arcsine and Arccosine
theorem_text:
Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $-1 \le x \le 1$.
Then:
$\arcsin x + \arccos x = \dfrac \pi 2$
where $\arcsin$ and $\arccos$ denote arcsine and arccosine respectively.
proof_text:
Let $y \in \R$ such that:
$\exists x \in \left[{-1 \,.\,.\, 1}\right]: x = \cos \left({y + \dfrac \pi 2}\right)$
Then:
$$x = \cos \left({y + \frac \pi 2}\right)$$
$$= -\sin y$$
Cosine of Angle plus Right Angle
$$= \sin \left({-y}\right)$$
Sine Function is Odd
Suppose $-\dfrac \pi 2 \le y \le \dfrac \pi 2$.
Then we can write $-y = \arcsin x$.
But then $\cos \left({y + \dfrac \pi 2}\right) = x$.
Now since $-\dfrac \pi 2 \le y \le \dfrac \pi 2$ it follows that $0 \le y + \dfrac \pi 2 \le \pi$.
Hence $y + \dfrac \pi 2 = \arccos x$.
That is, $\dfrac \pi 2 = \arccos x + \arcsin x$.
review_reason: As y runs through the stated symmetric interval, cos(y+pi/2) covers [-1,1]. The two indicated angles lie on the respective principal branches and sum to pi/2.

title: Complex Numbers form Field
theorem_text:
Consider the algebraic structure $\struct {\C, +, \times}$, where:
$\C$ is the set of all complex numbers
$+$ is the operation of complex addition
$\times$ is the operation of complex multiplication
Then $\struct {\C, +, \times}$ forms a field.
proof_text:
From Complex Numbers under Addition form Abelian Group, we have that $\struct {\C, +}$ forms an abelian group.
From Non-Zero Complex Numbers under Multiplication form Abelian Group, we have that $\struct {\C_{\ne 0}, \times}$ forms an abelian group.
Finally, we have that Complex Multiplication Distributes over Addition.
Thus all the criteria are fulfilled, and $\struct {\C, +, \times}$ is a field.
review_reason: The cited additive and nonzero multiplicative abelian groups and distributive law give the field axioms for the complex numbers.

title: Complex Modulus of Product of Complex Numbers
theorem_text:
Let $z_1, z_2 \in \C$ be complex numbers.
Let $\cmod z$ be the modulus of $z$.
Then:
$\cmod {z_1 z_2} = \cmod {z_1} \cdot \cmod {z_2}$
proof_text:
Let $\overline z$ denote the complex conjugate of $z$.
Then:
$$\cmod {z_1 z_2} = \sqrt {\paren {z_1 z_2} \overline {\paren {z_1 z_2} } }$$
Modulus in Terms of Conjugate
$$= \sqrt {z_1 \overline {z_1} z_2 \overline {z_2} }$$
Product of Complex Conjugates, Complex Multiplication is Commutative
$$= \sqrt {z_1 \overline {z_1} } \sqrt {z_2 \overline {z_2} }$$
Power of Product
$$= \cmod {z_1} \cmod {z_2}$$
review_reason: Conjugation preserves products, and each factor z times its conjugate is nonnegative real. Thus the nonnegative square root factors as the product of moduli.

title: Complex Plane is Metric Space
theorem_text:
Let $\C$ be the set of all complex numbers.
Let $d: \C \times \C \to \R$ be the function defined as:
$\map d {z_1, z_2} = \size {z_1 - z_2}$
where $\size z$ is the modulus of $z$.
Then $d$ is a metric on $\C$ and so $\struct {\C, d}$ is a metric space.
proof_text:
Let $z_1 = x_1 + i y_1, z_2 = x_2 + i y_2$.
From the definition of modulus:
$\size {z_1 - z_2} = \sqrt {\paren {x_1 - x_2}^2 + \paren {y_1 - y_2}^2}$
This is the euclidean metric on the real number plane
This is shown in Euclidean Metric on Real Vector Space is Metric to be a metric.
Thus the complex plane is a 2-dimensional Euclidean space.
review_reason: Identifying a complex number with its real and imaginary components turns the proposed distance into the known Euclidean metric.

title: Open Sets in Metric Space
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space.
Then $\O$ and $A$ are both open in $M$.
proof_text:
We have the results:
: Empty Set is Open in Metric Space
: Metric Space is Open in Itself
review_reason: The two cited metric-space results establish separately that the empty set and the entire underlying space are open.

title: Finite Intersection of Open Sets of Metric Space is Open
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space.
Let $U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n$ be open in $M$.
Then $\ds \bigcap_{i \mathop = 1}^n U_i$ is open in $M$.
That is, a finite intersection of open subsets is open.
proof_text:
Let $\ds x \in \bigcap_{i \mathop = 1}^n U_i$.
By the definition of intersection, for each $i \in \closedint 1 n$, we have $x \in U_i$.
Thus, since $U_i$ is open in $M$:
$\exists \epsilon_i > 0: \map {B_{\epsilon_i} } x \subseteq U_i$
where $\map {B_{\epsilon_i} } x$ is the open $\epsilon_i$-ball of $x$.
Let $\displaystyle \epsilon = \min_{i \mathop = 1}^n \set {\epsilon_i}$.
Then, by Open Ball contains Smaller Open Ball:
$\map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq \map {B_{\epsilon_i} } x$
for all $i \in \closedint 1 n$.
So:
$\ds \map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq \bigcap_{i \mathop = 1}^n U_i$
The result follows.
review_reason: At any point of the intersection the minimum of finitely many positive ball radii remains positive, and its ball lies in every set.

title: Union of Open Sets of Metric Space is Open
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space.
The union of a set of open sets of $M$ is open in $M$.
proof_text:
Let $I$ be any indexing set.
Let $U_i$ be open in $M$ for all $i \in I$.
Let $\ds x \in \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} U_i$.
Then by definition of set union, $x \in U_k$ for some $k \in I$.
Since $U_k$ is open in $M$:
$\ds \exists \epsilon > 0: \map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq U_k$
where $\map {B_\epsilon} x$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $M$.
By Set is Subset of Union:
$\ds U_k \subseteq \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} U_i$
Hence by Subset Relation is Transitive:
$\ds \map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} U_i$
and the result follows by definition of open set in metric space.
review_reason: A point of the union belongs to a particular open member, whose neighborhood ball also lies in the union. This argument is vacuous for the empty union.

title: Derivative of Function of Constant Multiple
theorem_text:
Let $f$ be a real function which is differentiable on $\R$.
Let $c \in \R$ be a constant.
Then:
$\map {D_x} {\map f {c x} } = c \map {D_{c x} } {\map f {c x} }$
proof_text:
First it is shown that $\map {D_x} {c x} = c$:
$$\map {D_x} {c x} = c \map {D_x} x + x \map {D_x} c$$
Product Rule
$$= c + x \map {D_x} c$$
Derivative of Identity Function
$$= c + 0$$
Derivative of Constant
$$= c$$
Next:
$$\map {D_x} {\map f {c x} } = \map {D_x} {c x} \map {D_{c x} } {\map f {c x} }$$
Chain Rule for Derivatives
$$= c \map {D_{c x} } {\map f {c x} }$$
from above
review_reason: The inner linear function has derivative c, and applying the chain rule to the composition gives c times the derivative of f evaluated at cx.

title: Indiscrete Topology is not Metrizable
theorem_text:
Let $S$ be a set with more than one element.
The indiscrete topology on $S$ is not metrizable.
proof_text:
In order to be metrizable, there needs to be a metric $d$ on $S$, so that $\struct {S, d}$ is a metric space.
As $S$ has more than one element, $\exists x, y \in S: x \ne y$.
Then:
$\epsilon = \map d {x, y} > 0$
So the open $\epsilon$-ball $\map {B_{\epsilon / 2} } x$ is $d$-open.
Hence $\map {B_{\epsilon / 2} } x$ is in the topology which $d$ induces.
But $x \in \map {B_{\epsilon / 2} } x$ while $y \notin \map {B_{\epsilon / 2} } x$.
Thus $\map {B_{\epsilon / 2} } x \ne \O$ and $\map {B_{\epsilon / 2} } x \ne S$.
So the topology induced by $d$ is not the indiscrete topology.
review_reason: A ball of radius half the distance between two distinct points contains one and omits the other. Such a nonempty proper open set cannot belong to an indiscrete topology.

title: Composite of Continuous Mappings is Continuous
theorem_text:
Let $T_1, T_2, T_3$ be topological spaces.
Let $f: T_1 \to T_2$ and $g: T_2 \to T_3$ be continuous mappings.
Then the composite mapping $g \circ f: T_1 \to T_3$ is continuous.
proof_text:
Let $U \in T_3$ be open in $T_3$.
As $g$ is continuous, $g^{-1} \sqbrk U \in T_2$ is open in $T_2$.
As $f$ is continuous, $f^{-1} \sqbrk {g^{-1} \sqbrk U} \in T_1$ is open in $T_1$.
By Inverse of Composite Bijection, $f^{-1} \sqbrk {g^{-1} \sqbrk U} = \paren {g \circ f}^{-1} \sqbrk U$.
Hence the result.
review_reason: Successive preimages of an open set are open and give its preimage under the composite. This preimage identity follows directly by membership for all functions, despite the reference to a result about bijections.

title: Continuity Test using Basis
theorem_text:
Let $\left({X_1, \tau_1}\right)$ and $\left({X_2, \tau_2}\right)$ be topological spaces.
Let $f: X_1 \to X_2$ be a mapping.
Let $\mathcal B$ be an analytic basis for $\tau_2$.
Suppose that:
$\forall B \in \mathcal B: f^{-1} \left({B}\right) \in \tau_1$
where $f^{-1} \left({B}\right)$ denotes the preimage of $B$ under $f$.
Then $f$ is continuous.
proof_text:
Let $U \in \tau_2$.
By the definition of an analytic basis, it follows that:
$\displaystyle \exists \mathcal A \subseteq \mathcal B: U = \bigcup \mathcal A$
Hence:
$$f^{-1} \left({U}\right) = f^{-1} \left({\bigcup \mathcal A}\right)$$
$$= \bigcup_{B \mathop \in \mathcal A} f^{-1} \left({B}\right)$$
Preimage of Union under Mapping: General Result
$$\in \tau_1$$
by hypothesis, and by the definition of a topology
The result follows from the definition of continuity.
review_reason: Every target open set is a union of basis elements. Taking its preimage gives a union of open preimages, hence an open set.

title: Epimorphism Preserves Distributivity
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {R_1, +_1, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {R_2, +_2, \circ_2}$ be algebraic structures.
Let $\phi: R_1 \to R_2$ be an epimorphism.
:If $\circ_1$ is left distributive over $+_1$, then $\circ_2$ is left distributive over $+_2$.
:If $\circ_1$ is right distributive over $+_1$, then $\circ_2$ is right distributive over $+_2$.
Consequently, if $\circ_1$ is distributive over $+_1$, then $\circ_2$ is distributive over $+_2$.
That is, epimorphism preserves distributivity.
proof_text:
Throughout the following, we assume the morphism property holds for $\phi$ for both operations.
Left Distributivity
Suppose $\circ_1$ is left distributive over $+_1$. Then:
$$\map \phi x \circ_2 \paren {\map \phi y +_2 \map \phi z} = \map \phi x \circ_2 \map \phi {y +_1 z}$$
$$= \map \phi {x \circ_1 \paren {y +_1 z} }$$
$$= \map \phi {\paren {x \circ_1 y} +_1 \paren {x \circ_1 z} }$$
as $\circ_1$ is left distributive over $+_1$
$$= \map \phi {x \circ_1 y} +_2 \phi \paren {x \circ_1 z}$$
$$= \paren {\map \phi x \circ_2 \map \phi y} +_2 \paren {\map \phi x \circ_2 \map \phi z}$$
So $\circ_2$ is left distributive over $+_2$.
Right Distributivity
Suppose $\circ_1$ is right distributive over $+_1$. Then:
$$\paren {\map \phi x +_2 \map \phi y} \circ_2 \map \phi z = \map \phi {x +_1 y} \circ_2 \map \phi z$$
$$= \map \phi {\paren {x +_1 y} \circ_1 z}$$
$$= \map \phi {\paren {x \circ_1 z} +_1 \paren {y \circ_1 z} }$$
as $\circ_1$ is right distributive over $+_1$
$$= \map \phi {x \circ_1 z} +_2 \map \phi {y \circ_1 z}$$
$$= \paren {\map \phi x \circ_2 \map \phi z} +_2 \paren {\map \phi y \circ_2 \map \phi z}$$
So $\circ_2$ is right distributive over $+_2$.
Distributivity
If $\circ_1$ is distributive over $+_1$, then it is both right and left distributive over $+_1$.
Hence from the above, $\circ_2$ is both right and left distributive over $+_2$.
That is, $\circ_2$ is distributive over $+_2$.
review_reason: The calculations transport the left and right identities through a homomorphism of both operations. Under the surjective meaning of epimorphism used here every target triple has preimages.

title: Epimorphism Preserves Groups
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be algebraic structures.
Let $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ be an epimorphism.
Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a group.
Then $\struct {T, *}$ is also a group.
proof_text:
From Epimorphism Preserves Semigroups, if $\struct {S, \circ}$ is a semigroup then so is $\struct {T, *}$.
From Epimorphism Preserves Identity, if $\struct {S, \circ}$ has an identity $e_S$, then $\map \phi {e_S}$ is the identity for $*$.
From Epimorphism Preserves Inverses, if $x^{-1}$ is an inverse of $x$ for $\circ$, then $\map \phi {x^{-1} }$ is an inverse of $\map \phi x$ for $*$.
The result follows from the definition of group.
review_reason: Associativity and identity pass to the image, as do inverses of all preimages. Surjectivity makes these properties hold throughout the target.

title: Totally Bounded Metric Space is Bounded
theorem_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a totally bounded metric space.
Then $M$ is bounded.
proof_text:
Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be totally bounded.
Then there exist $n \in \N$ and points $x_0, \dots, x_n \in A$ such that:
$\displaystyle \inf_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \map d {x_i, x} \le 1$
for all $x \in A$.
Let us set:
$a := x_0$
$\displaystyle D := \max_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \map d {x_0, x_i}$
$K := D + 1$
Now let $x \in A$ be arbitrary.
Then by assumption there exists $i$ such that $\map d {x_i, x} \le 1$.
Hence:
$\map d {a, x} \le \map d {a, x_i} + \map d {x_i, x} \le 1 + D = K$
So $M$ is bounded, as claimed.
review_reason: A finite unit net has a maximum distance from a chosen center to all the other centers. The triangle inequality adds at most one to reach any point. The empty space is vacuously bounded.

title: Projection from Product Topology is Continuous
theorem_text:
Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces.
Let $T = \struct {T_1 \times T_2, \tau}$ be the product space of $T_1$ and $T_2$, where $\tau$ is the Tychonoff topology on $S$.
Let $\pr_1: T \to T_1$ and $\pr_2: T \to T_2$ be the first and second projections from $T$ onto its factors.
Then both $\pr_1$ and $\pr_2$ are are continuous.
proof_text:
From Natural Basis of Tychonoff Topology:Finite Product, a basis for $\tau$ is:
$\BB = \set {U \times V: U \in \tau_1, V \in \tau_2}$
et $U$ be open in $T_1$.
Then $\map {\pr_1^{-1} } U = U \times T_2$ is one of the open sets in the basis in the definition of product topology.
Thus $\pr_1$ is continuous.
The same argument can be applied to $\pr_2$.
review_reason: The preimage of an open set under a projection is its product with the entire other factor and is open in the product topology, for either projection.

title: Open and Closed Sets in Topological Space
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space.
Then $S$ and $\O$ are both both open and closed in $T$.
proof_text:
From the definition of closed set, $U$ is open in $T$ if and only if $S \setminus U$ is closed in $T$.
From Underlying Set of Topological Space is Clopen, $S$ is both open and closed in $T$.
From Empty Set is Element of Topology, $\O$ is open in $T$.
From Empty Set is Closed in Topological Space, we have that $\O$ is closed in $T$.
review_reason: The cited results give openness and closedness of the full space and the empty set, which are complements of one another.

title: Absolutely Continuous Real Function is Continuous
theorem_text:
Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a real interval.
Let $f : I \to \R$ be an absolutely continuous function.
Then $f$ is continuous.
proof_text:
From Absolutely Continuous Real Function is Uniformly Continuous:
$f$ is uniformly continuous.
Therefore, from Uniformly Continuous Real Function is Continuous:
$f$ is continuous.
review_reason: Absolute continuity on the interval implies uniform continuity there, and uniform continuity implies pointwise continuity.

title: Real Numbers are Uncountable
theorem_text: The set of real numbers $\R$ is uncountably infinite.
proof_text:
By definition, a perfect set is a set $X$ such that every point $x \in X$ is the limit of a sequence of points of $X$ distinct from $x$.
From Real Numbers form Perfect Set, $\R$ is perfect.
Therefore it is sufficient to show that a perfect subset of $X \subseteq \R^k$ is uncountable.
We prove the equivalent result that every sequence $\sequence {x_k}_{k \mathop \in \N} \subseteq X$ omits at least one point in $X$.
Let $y_1 \in X$.
Let $B_1:= \map {\BB_r} {y_1}$ be a closed ball centred at $y_1$.
Consider a closed ball:
$B_{n - 1} \supseteq B_n := \map {\BB_{\map \delta n} } {y_n}$
such that:
$\map \delta n \le \dfrac {\map \delta {n - 1} } 2$
$y_n \in X$
$x_n \notin B_n$
Note that $\map \delta 1 = r$.
We can satisfy the condition $x_n \notin B_n$ because $X$ is perfect, so every ball centred at a point of $X$ contains infinitely many points of $X$.
Since $\map \delta n \le \dfrac r {2^{n - 1} }$, $y_n$ is Cauchy.
Therefore from Perfect Set is Closed, we may let $\displaystyle Y = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} y_n \in X$.
For $n \in \N$ we have:
$\set {y_m: m > n} \subseteq B_n$
so $Y \in B_n$.
But by construction:
$\forall n \in \N: x_n \notin B_n$
Therefore:
$\forall n \in \N: Y \ne x_n$
and the proof is complete.
review_reason: Nested closed balls with radii tending to zero can be chosen to avoid each listed real in turn. Their centers converge by Euclidean completeness, and their common point cannot occur on the list; the real line is itself closed.

title: Real Numbers are Uncountable
theorem_text: The set of real numbers $\R$ is uncountably infinite.
proof_text:
It is sufficient to show that the real interval $I = \set {x \in \R: 0 < x \le 1}$ is uncountable.
Let $x \in I$.
From Existence of Base-N Representation, $x$ has a unique representation of the form:
$x = \dfrac {\epsilon_1} 3 + \dfrac {\epsilon_2} {3^2} + \dfrac {\epsilon_3} {3^3} + \cdots$
where $\epsilon_k = 0, 1$ or $2$ and an infinite number of $\epsilon_k$ are different from $0$.
Let $S \subseteq I$ be countably infinite.
Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots}$.
Let $\epsilon_{k 1}, \epsilon_{k 2}, \epsilon_{k 3}, \ldots$ be the ternary digits of $x_k$.
Let $\epsilon_k = 1 + 2 \epsilon_{k k} - \epsilon_{k k}^2$ so that:
$\epsilon_k = 1$ if $\epsilon_{k k} = 0$ or $\epsilon_{k k} = 2$
$\epsilon_k = 2$ if $\epsilon_{k k} = 1$
Then:
$(1): \quad \forall k: \epsilon_k \ne 0$
$(2): \quad \forall k: \epsilon_k \ne \epsilon_{k k}$
We have that $0 < x \le 1$ so $x \in I$.
But the real number $\displaystyle x = \sum \epsilon_k 3^{-k}$ is different from every $x_k \in I$.
Thus we have found an element of $I$ which is not an element of $S$.
Therefore $S$ is a proper subset of $I$.
It follows by definition that $I$ is uncountable.
review_reason: The constructed ternary digit is nonzero and differs from the kth listed number in position k. Selecting nonterminating representations ensures distinct such digit strings represent distinct numbers.

title: Condition for Point being in Closure
theorem_text:
Let $T$ be a topological space.
Let $H \subseteq T$.
Let $x \in T$.
Then $x \in H^-$ if and only if every open set of $T$ which contains $x$ contains a point in $H$.
proof_text:
From the definition of closure, we have that $H^-$ is the union of $H$ and all the limit points of $H$ in $T$.
Necessary Condition
Suppose $x \in H^-$.
Then either:
$(1): \quad x \in H$, in which case every open set of $T$ which contains $x$ trivially contains a point in $H$ (that is, $x$ itself);
$(2): \quad x$ is a limit point of $H$ in $T$.
If the latter is the case, then it follows directly from the definition of limit point that every open set of $T$ which contains $x$ contains a point in $H$ other than $x$.
Sufficient Condition
Suppose that every open set of $T$ which contains $x$ contains a point in $H$.
If $x \in H$, then $x$ is in the union of $H$ and all the limit points of $H$ in $T$.
Hence by definition $x \in H^-$.
If $x \notin H$ then $x$ must be a limit point of $H$ by definition.
So again, $x$ is in the union of $H$ and all the limit points of $H$ in $T$.
Hence by definition $x \in H^-$.
review_reason: Membership in H handles the neighborhood condition directly. Outside H the condition is exactly the definition of a limit point, giving both directions.

title: Topological Closure of Subset is Subset of Topological Closure
theorem_text:
Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space.
Let $H \subseteq K$ and $K \subseteq S$.
Then:
$\map \cl H \subseteq \map \cl K$
where $\map \cl H$ denotes the closure of $H$.
proof_text:
From Topological Closure is Closed, $\map \cl K$ is closed.
From Set is Subset of its Topological Closure:
$K \subseteq \map \cl K$
By Subset Relation is Transitive, it follows that:
$H \subseteq \map \cl K$
Hence, by definition of closure as the smallest closed set that contains $H$:
$\map \cl H \subseteq \map \cl K$
review_reason: The closure of K is a closed set containing H, hence contains the smallest such closed set, the closure of H.
